tracks.title: A bot is a public address
tracks.text: Lesson two point eleven — channels. A sub-lesson, under nexus. Here's what you want. You want to text your engine. Message your agent on Telegram… ask it for a deploy status… tell it to kick off a run. [curious] And every mainstream way to do that is scary in the same two ways. First — the token. The standard recipe pastes a bot token into the code that does the talking. So the workload holds the secret. And the workload is exactly the thing that fetches untrusted pages, runs generated code, and reads model output. Give it the credential, and one leak — or one prompt injection — walks the token right out the door. Second — the door itself. A bot is a public address. Anyone who finds it can speak into your system… and in the agent era, that's not spam. That's an injection front door — a stranger putting text upstream of a worker that acts on text. [curious] This lesson fixes both. And it's honest about exactly where the work stops.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A channel is a runtime capability module. An adapter that does three things — it reports whether it's configured… it sends outbound messages… and it runs a supervised inbound poller. And it's registered host-side, on the engine. Its credential lives in the engine's environment… never in workbook or sandbox content. The source calls this the official-API tier — and that phrase earns its keep. The Telegram adapter talks to the real Bot API. Nothing reverse-engineered… nothing scraped out of a logged-in client. A channel is configured exactly when its adapter finds its credential. And only a configured channel accepts sends or starts its poller. [curious] Today the registry holds one entry — telegram. Adding another is a new module, plus one line. We'll get there.

tracks.title: Why it lives host-side
tracks.text: Next — why it lives host-side. The whole design turns on one boundary you've met — the Dock. The membrane between the engine and the workload it runs. A channel sits on the engine side of that membrane. The workload never holds the token… never makes the call. It asks the engine to send… and the engine decides, and does it. Picture the two approaches side by side — and the difference isn't comfort, it's blast radius. Take the first row — a bot library living inside your app. The token sits in the workload, in code that runs untrusted input. The workload polls. And if that workload is compromised, the token is exfiltrated — the bot is now the attacker's. Now the second row — a channel in the engine. The token sits in host-side environment, and it never crosses the Dock. A supervised host process does the polling, where the workload can't even see it. And if the workload is compromised? It can request a send… that's all. It cannot steal the token… and it cannot read the wire. [excited] The verdict of that table in one line — the workload's reach ends at, ask the engine to send this. It can never become the bot.

tracks.title: Config is topology
tracks.text: Config is topology. And here's the part that surprises people. The configured check doesn't just gate whether a send is allowed. It gates whether the inbound poller exists as a running process at all. Let me read you the gate — it's the whole feature flag, one conditional in the supervision tree. The function is called channels. It says — if the Telegram adapter is configured, return a list holding the Telegram poller… else, return an empty list. And configured itself is one line — the token is set when it is not nil and not empty. The token comes straight from the environment variable. Now picture the engine booting, building its child list, and hitting one fork. The question — is the bot token set? Down the yes branch — the poller joins the supervision tree, starts long-polling Telegram, and the send and approve routes answer for real. Down the no branch — the module stays inert code, no poller in the tree, and the routes answer… not configured. [curious] No half-on state. No dormant daemon. Topology follows the environment. And this is a house idiom — call it the keeper pattern. Four optional children gated the very same way, at one line each. First, the keeper — gated by its agent definition. Second, the autopoet — gated by its env flag. Third, the groundskeeper — gated by its secret. And fourth, channels — gated by the bot token. In every case… unset the credential, the child is excluded. The credential is the feature flag.

tracks.title: The pairing ceremony
tracks.text: Now the centerpiece — the pairing ceremony. The DM policy is a pairing-code allowlist. Default-deny… with a human in the loop. An unknown sender never reaches the inbox. They get a short code, and they get parked. A human approves. And only then do their messages land. Walk it with me. A stranger messages the bot. The adapter checks the sender — neither approved nor pending — so it mints a code. Crypto-random bytes, Base-thirty-two encoded, cut to six characters. Not a counter… real randomness. It parks them in pending, and replies, word for word — Workbooks pairing code, J five K two Q A. Approve with… wb channels approve telegram, J five K two Q A. The stranger messages again. [chuckles] And they get the same code. The check is idempotent — an already-pending peer keeps its existing code, instead of minting a fresh one every message. Still nothing in the inbox. Now the operator runs the approve verb. That moves the peer into approved, de-duplicated… and deletes the code. A pairing code is single-use — consumed on approval. And the next message from that peer, now allowed, appends one line to the inbox. [curious] Two honest absences, both on purpose. There is no revoke verb — un-approving someone today means editing the file by hand. And there's no expiry on a pending code — it sits there until it's approved or you delete it. The ceremony is small… and these are the edges of small.

tracks.title: Two files on disk
tracks.text: A depth rung now — two files on disk. The whole policy is two human-greppable files per channel, under the channels folder in your data directory. That directory is a temp folder in development… and the mounted volume when deployed. So state is restart-proof either way — approve someone once, and they stay approved across reboots. Picture the two files as a small table. The first file is the allow-file. Its shape — an approved list of peers, and a pending map of code to peer. It's written by the sender check when it mints a code, and by approve when it moves a peer and deletes the code. And it's read by every single inbound message, to decide… allowed, or pairing. The second file is the inbox — JSONL, one inbound message per line. It's written by the append step, only on an allowed message. And what reads it? [curious] Nothing yet. That's this slice's terminus. Let me read you the allow-file across an approval. Before — approved is empty, and pending holds J five K two Q A pointing at peer five-five-nine-eight-eight-two-one. After — approved holds that peer… and pending is empty. The code crossed over, and then vanished. And one allowed message is one line. The Telegram record carries — a second-resolution timestamp… the channel, telegram… the peer, a stringified chat id… the sender's username, if any… the text… and Telegram's own update id. [excited] You can read your entire messaging state with cat. That's not a toy property — it's the same posture as everything here. Plain text you can inspect, diff, and edit by hand when a verb doesn't exist yet.

tracks.title: Inside the poller
tracks.text: Another depth rung — inside the poller. The Telegram adapter is one module wearing two hats. Outbound, it's a function that calls the Bot API's send-message. Inbound, it's a supervised, long-running process that calls get-updates in a loop. Long-poll… not webhooks — which means no inbound HTTP surface to expose. The engine reaches out and holds a connection open. Nothing has to reach in. That's what lets a channel work behind a private control plane, with nothing published to the internet. The loop is a few deliberate numbers — let me give you each with its reason. First, the server-side hold — twenty-five seconds. Get-updates waits that long for a message. One patient request, not a busy poll. Second, the re-loop on success — zero milliseconds. Go straight back around, because the request itself already held twenty-five seconds. Third, the backoff on error — five seconds. A failed call waits before retrying, so we don't hammer a sick API. Fourth, the transport timeout — thirty-five seconds. The HTTP client has to outlive the twenty-five second hold… so thirty-five is greater than twenty-five, on purpose. And fifth, the offset — the max update id, plus one. Acknowledge what you got… and on an empty batch, fall back to offset minus one. Picture the loop. Poll — hold up to twenty-five seconds. Then a fork — any updates? Down the yes branch — handle each one. Allowed goes to the inbox… unknown gets the pairing reply… a non-message update is ignored. Then advance the offset, and loop. Down the no-or-error branch — log a warning, wait five seconds, and loop. [curious] Three details earn their place. The token is path material in the API URL — so the adapter is written to keep it out of logs. A leaked log line shouldn't be a leaked credential. Any exception inside the loop is rescued — so a malformed update never kills the poller. It warns, backs off, goes again. The channel stays up. And non-message updates — edits, joins, the housekeeping Telegram sends — are simply ignored. And the transport is the built-in HTTP client, with the HTTP layer injectable — tests pass a stub, so the whole suite runs with zero network and no real token. That's how the pairing policy and the inbox are proven… without ever touching Telegram.

tracks.title: Driving it
tracks.text: Driving it. Two surfaces, both behind the engine's auth — the control plane is authed end to end. Picture the verbs as a small table. First — wb channels list, hitting GET slash api slash channels. On success it returns the channels and whether each is configured. Second — wb channels send, hitting POST send. On success, ok true and the sent message. On failure — an unknown channel is a four hundred… and a not-configured channel comes back unavailable. Third — wb channels approve, hitting POST approve. On success, ok true and the peer. On failure — no pending code is a four oh four. The CLI runs against the connected runtime, the same target resolution as wb rt — a runtime URL and token if set, otherwise the local discovery file. The creds and the pollers live there, on the engine… not in the CLI. A real session — you run wb channels list, and it answers with telegram, configured true. You run wb channels send telegram, the peer, and the text, build green — shipped. And it answers ok true, sent, telegram, that peer. [chuckles] And the failures are honest. Send to a channel with no token — channel not configured, telegram. Send to one that isn't even in the registry — the test literally uses carrier-pigeon — and you get, unknown channel, with a four hundred. Two error atoms, two clear answers. The registry didn't know it… or the credential wasn't there.

tracks.title: Where the slice ends
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where the slice ends. And this is a real boundary, not a hedge. This shipped as Channels slice one. And the slice stops at the inbox. Approved messages land as JSONL lines — and nothing reads them yet. No get-inbox route… no consumer anywhere in the codebase. Routing the inbox to an agent session is deliberately not wired in this slice — the source says so, right there in a comment. The inbox is, in its own words, this slice's terminus. The rest of the honest list follows from being slice one. There is exactly one adapter — Telegram. The registry is a compile-time map — so adding a channel means a new module and one line… it isn't pluggable at runtime. There's no revoke verb, and no pending-code expiry — so the allow-file gets edited by hand for those, today. And the inbox grows unbounded — nothing rotates it. Long-poll, not webhooks — a choice with a cost. One held connection per channel… in exchange for needing no public inbound surface. [curious] Here's the frame that matters. The shape is finished. The routing is the frontier. The durable thing this page sells is the shape — a capability on the engine side of the membrane, gated by its own credential, fronted by a default-deny allowlist with a human in the loop. That shape is done, and proven. Where an approved message goes next — into a worker, through dispatch — that's the part still being built. And we'd rather point at it… than paper over it.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Where does the token live — can a workbook read it? Host-side, in the engine's environment. And no — it never crosses the Dock into the sandbox. The workload can ask the engine to send… it can't read the token or touch the wire. Can anyone DM my bot? Anyone can send to it — a handle is public. But a stranger only ever sees a six-character pairing code and a one-line instruction. Their messages don't land until a human approves. The open handle is harmless, because the door behind it isn't. What about group chats? A group has a chat id, and the policy keys on chat id — so the same pairing-then-approve flow applies to any chat. Whether groups are an intended use is genuinely open… the mechanism just doesn't care which kind of chat a peer is. How do I un-approve someone? Today, by hand — edit the allow-file, remove them from approved. No revoke verb in this slice. [chuckles] And why polling, not webhooks? Because a webhook needs a public inbound endpoint… and the whole point is to run behind a private control plane with nothing published. Long-poll reverses the direction — the engine holds a connection out, so no stranger can reach in.

tracks.title: Back up to nexus
tracks.text: So that's channels. Not a clever bot trick — a capability, on the engine side of the membrane. The token never crosses into the workload. Config is topology — the credential's presence is what puts the poller in the running system. And a stranger gets a pairing code… never your inbox. [curious] The way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under nexus — the engine and the membrane it all sits on. From there, two siblings share this exact posture. Secrets — the same host-side handling, for your workload's credentials. And keepers — the env-gated supervision idiom this lesson borrowed its name from. Everything channels does… is one capability among several, behind one membrane. Start with nexus, and the rest falls into place.
